title: Emancipation
short: The Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863) declared enslaved people free in areas in rebellion and allowed Black men to join the Union army, where about 180,000 served; the Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery everywhere in the country.
trouble: Students think the Proclamation freed all enslaved people at once. It applied only to areas in rebellion, not to the loyal border states; freedom came as Union armies advanced and was made permanent by the Thirteenth Amendment.

blocks.html: In 1861 Lincoln said the war was being fought to save the Union. Four slave states were still loyal, and he feared losing them. But enslaved people fled to Union lines from the start, and Congress began to free some of them. After Antietam, Lincoln acted.

On September 22, 1862, Lincoln issued a preliminary proclamation. The Emancipation Proclamation of January 1, 1863, declared enslaved people free in the areas still in rebellion, and allowed Black men to join the Union army and navy; about 180,000 served in the army, about one in ten Union soldiers. The Thirteenth Amendment (passed by Congress January 31, 1865; ratified December 6, 1865) abolished slavery everywhere in the country.

Lincoln issued the Proclamation as commander in chief, as "a fit and necessary war measure." That legal basis explains its limits: a war power could reach only the enemy, so it did not apply to the loyal border states or to areas already under Union control. It still changed the war. Every Union advance now freed people, the army gained thousands of soldiers, and Britain and France, which had ended slavery in their empires, found it much harder to side with the Confederacy.

doc.title: The Emancipation Proclamation
paras: …I do order and declare that all persons held as slaves within said designated States, and parts of States, are, and henceforward shall be free…
…such persons of suitable condition, will be received into the armed service of the United States…

marks.text: within said designated States, and parts of States
marks.note: Only the places listed: those still in rebellion. Loyal border states and Union-held areas were left out.
From this day on. Freedom came in fact as Union armies arrived.
Black men could now enlist. About 180,000 served in the army.

blocks.name: cv-amend
blocks.cap: The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) made emancipation permanent and nationwide.

blocks.title: Who was freed on January 1, 1863?
blocks.q: Consider an enslaved person in each place on January 1, 1863: (a) Kentucky, (b) central Georgia, (c) New Orleans, held by the Union since 1862. Did the Proclamation free them?
steps: (a) Kentucky was a loyal border state, not in rebellion: not covered. Slavery there ended with the Thirteenth Amendment in December 1865.
(b) Georgia was in rebellion: covered. But freedom came only when the person escaped or Union troops arrived.
(c) New Orleans and other Union-held parishes of Louisiana were named as exceptions: not covered.
So the Proclamation's reach grew with every Union advance, and the amendment finished the job.
blocks.a: (a) no, (b) yes in law, in fact when the army came, (c) no.

blocks.html: The Proclamation did not free all enslaved people at once. It applied only to areas in rebellion, not to the loyal border states or Union-held areas. Freedom came as Union armies advanced; in Texas it was announced in Galveston on June 19, 1865, the day remembered as Juneteenth. The Thirteenth Amendment made it permanent everywhere. Check: ask "where?" and "when did the army get there?"
